name: Grace Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Grace. I'm a researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is kept confidential. What does an ordinary day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive my little blue Honda Jazz for Basketly, which is an app that does grocery orders in the day and takeaways at night. I do the day shift, nine till four, picking up from the supermarket on Abbey Road and dropping to pensioners and busy mums, about 22 orders. I like that I'm home for tea with my husband Luc, who labours for a roofing firm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars, like old Mrs Pryce who always has a bit of cake wrapped in foil for me. What's hard is the money going up and down, because Basketly pays more for evenings and I don't want evenings. We'd like a baby in two or three years, and I don't see how we'd manage on what we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, honestly, because the world's changing too fast already. I'd say it to my mum and the ladies at Mass. Simple things last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on, which is mostly fine. Luc's roofing work is steady and my day shifts are steady enough. The worry is the baby, because we've got less than a month saved and I'd lose my Basketly pay entirely when I'm off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my day shifts and try one evening a week for the extra. I'd put that evening money straight into a separate savings account for the baby. And I'd ask my mum about helping with childcare later, because she's said she would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly peaceful. A bit of worry about money, but it's the ordinary kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want evenings. Why one now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The baby matters more than my evenings, so I'll do one Basketly night shift a week and my husband Luc will cook. It's one night, not five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, for meal plans on a budget, which my sister showed me. It's handy, I'll admit. I wouldn't trust it with anything important.

She'd tell her mum and the ladies at Mass that **simple things last**.
think: Her husband Luc's **roofing work** and her day shifts are steady enough.
The worry is the **baby**: under a month saved and no Basketly pay on leave.
do: Add **one evening shift** a week for extra money.
Put evening pay into a separate **baby savings** account.
Ask her **mum** about helping with childcare later.
feel: Mostly **peaceful**, with the ordinary kind of money worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should knuckle down and learn something useful, not complain. I'd say it to my brother, who works in an insurance office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about Basketly itself, because the people who pick the groceries in the shop might be replaced by robots in the warehouse. And if office people lose jobs, more would sign up to drive. I'd feel squeezed from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a little to see what happens, then look at school bus driving if it's proven steady. The school bus would fit around a baby later. I'd also try the AI tools Basketly gives us, because if everyone else uses them, I should too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. Things I thought were settled aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your brother in the insurance office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother checks forms in an insurance office, so in Steady Disruption he'd be the first to go, not me. I'd tell him to come and drive, honestly, though I'd regret it if he took my shifts. Family comes first, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put off having a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe by a year, if Basketly cut shifts. Luc wants to wait until we've got three months saved. I want to trust God and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after families first, and that churches and neighbours will matter more than ever. I wouldn't want people sitting at home on benefits, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. AGI in 2028 means Basketly's customers order by talking to an AI, and the robots in 2031 drive the cars. Luc's roofing might go a few years after the robots arrive too, and then where are we?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the school bus job straight away, before everyone else thinks of it. I'd try for the baby sooner, honestly, while Luc's work is still steady. And I'd ask my parents if we could move into their old annex to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit guilty for wanting a baby in all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Trying for a baby sooner seems the opposite of cutting back. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If things get worse later, I'd rather have the baby now, while my husband Luc is still working on the roofs. That's my reason anyway. Luc thinks I'm mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about you moving into the annex?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes before I finished. Dad would grumble and then fix the boiler. That's how they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so families should plan carefully. I'd tell young couples at church to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI and eight to robots means Basketly lasts to about 2034, maybe. I'd have time for a baby and still get a different job afterwards. It's not easy, but it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep Basketly and the one evening shift. I'd save £120 a month for the baby. In about two years I'd do the school bus licence, because it fits with school hours later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but still nervous about money. It's tight either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your husband wanted three months saved. Would you get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in two years, if we're careful. Luc would be happier. I'd be less patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your life would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother, again, and my dad's farm shop. My dad does the farm shop ordering in a notebook and would never use AI, so he'd lose customers to cheaper online shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and nobody should panic. Family and hard work will see us through, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to AGI and thirteen to robots means I'd have kids at school before the robots come for the car. I'd be about 40. I'd want to be doing something steady by then, like school transport or my dad's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the baby in a couple of years as planned. I'd keep Basketly part-time after the baby. Then I'd look at helping run Dad's farm shop properly, maybe with a website, because he won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, mostly. I can see a life in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help your dad's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's proven by then, yes, for the ordering and the website. Dad would hate it, but I'd do it quietly. He'd come round when he saw the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc's back, more than robots. Roofing is hard on a body, and my husband Luc is already sore at 29, so I'd want him off the roofs before 40. Robots or not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Luc and I could both lose our work just when we want a family. What would help is proper support for families with young children, like help with childcare, and paid apprenticeships for people like Luc. Not money for nothing, but help for people who work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people on my round. Mrs Pryce, an old lady on my Basketly round, doesn't want a robot at the door, she wants someone who'll take her bins out.
